issues.legal_issue: The pre-amendment criminal prohibition on benami transactions was unconstitutional because it imposed an excessively broad and harsh offence without essential safeguards.
material_facts: The former criminal provision applied on proof that one person paid or provided consideration for property held by another, without requiring proof of mens rea or that the ostensible holder lacked beneficial interest.
The provision was never implemented, and its gaps could not be supplied by judicial interpretation without changing its express terms.
The amended law restored a mens rea requirement and included a beneficial-interest element for the relevant category of transactions.
issues.conclusion: The Court declared the criminal provision in the unamended Act unconstitutional for manifest arbitrariness; it also held the corresponding provision in the amended Act unconstitutional insofar as it imposed punishment for past transactions, contrary to Article 20(1).
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 14, 19 and 21, legislation may be invalidated for manifest arbitrariness, including where it is irrational, excessive or lacks adequate safeguards; a criminal offence ordinarily requires mens rea unless its exclusion is clearly justified. The Court relied on Nathulal v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1966 SC 43, for the mens rea principle, and on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248, K. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, and Shayara Bano v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 1, for constitutional review and manifest arbitrariness. It also applied Article 20(1).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legacy_crimi: A constitutional challenge is brought to a criminal prohibition on benami transactions in an earlier statutory regime.
predicates.offence_definition_omits_mens_rea: The offence can be established without proving that the person acted with a guilty mind.
predicates.offence_definition_omits_beneficial_inte: The offence does not require proof that the person providing consideration retained a beneficial interest in the property.
predicates.criminal_rule_lacks_safeguards: The criminal provision lacks safeguards needed to prevent its overly broad or harsh application.

issues.definition: When a challenged legacy criminal offence omits mens rea and beneficial-interest requirements and lacks safeguards, the rule treats that offence as unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: The former statutory provision for acquiring benami property was unconstitutional because it left essential features of property-forfeiture proceedings undefined and without adequate safeguards.
material_facts: The former provision made benami property liable to acquisition without providing an operative procedure or adjudicatory mechanism.
Essential matters, including the standard of proof, the opportunity to establish a defence, the treatment of innocent owners and the vesting of property, were left to delegated rules.
The acquisition provision was never used.
issues.conclusion: The Court declared the former provision for in rem acquisition of benami property unconstitutional for manifest arbitrariness.
issues.legal_principle: A law authorizing deprivation or forfeiture of property must provide adequate safeguards and cannot leave essential features of the scheme to uncontrolled delegation. The Court relied on Articles 14, 19 and 21 and the manifest-arbitrariness principles discussed in K. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, Shayara Bano v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 1, and Joseph Shine v. Union of India, (2019) 3 SCC 39.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legacy_prope: A constitutional challenge is brought to an earlier statutory rule authorizing acquisition of property treated as benami.
predicates.acquisition_rule_omits_adjudicatory_mech: The acquisition rule does not itself provide an adequate adjudicatory process for deciding whether property is liable to acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_rule_omits_essential_safegua: The rule leaves essential matters, such as the standard of proof, available defences or protection of innocent owners, without adequate safeguards.

issues.definition: When an earlier property-acquisition rule is challenged and omits both an adjudicatory mechanism and essential safeguards, the rule treats that acquisition rule as unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: The amendments created substantive legal rules rather than merely supplying procedures for enforcing the earlier regime.
material_facts: The amended law substantially expanded the definition of benami transactions and property, including arrangements, fictitious transactions and transactions involving proceeds.
The amended law created a detailed attachment, adjudication and confiscation scheme and changed the evidentiary standard applicable to confiscation proceedings.
The earlier criminal and acquisition provisions were unconstitutional and had not been implemented.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the amendments were not merely procedural and that they prescribed substantive provisions.
issues.legal_principle: A change that creates new categories of prohibited conduct, alters substantive rights or changes evidentiary standards is substantive rather than merely procedural. Article 20(1) prohibits retroactive criminal liability; the Court distinguished procedural gap-filling from the creation of new substantive rules and relied on T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe, (1983) 1 SCC 177, and R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, (1995) 2 SCC 630, in considering retrospectivity and the earlier statutory regime.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_retroactive_applicat: A proceeding requires deciding whether statutory amendments apply to conduct or property dealings that predate their operation.
predicates.amendments_expand_prohibited_conduct: The amendments bring additional types of conduct or transactions within the prohibition.
predicates.amendments_change_substantive_property_o: The amendments alter rights relating to property or change the standard by which liability is determined.

issues.definition: When amendments are invoked against earlier conduct and expand prohibited conduct while altering substantive rights or evidentiary standards, the rule treats them as substantive rather than merely procedural.

issues.legal_issue: The amended criminal provisions cannot impose liability for transactions that occurred before the amended law came into force.
material_facts: The transaction concerning the property occurred before the amended law came into force.
The earlier criminal provision was unconstitutional and could not supply a valid offence for the earlier transaction.
The amended law created substantive criminal rules and included a separate penalty regime for transactions in the earlier period.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the amended criminal provisions operate prospectively, that the earlier unconstitutional offence could not be revived retroactively, and that applying the amended offence to earlier transactions would violate Article 20(1).
issues.legal_principle: Article 20(1) prohibits conviction under an ex post facto criminal law that creates an offence or increases punishment; an unconstitutional earlier criminal provision cannot be retroactively invigorated by later legislation. The Court relied on T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe, (1983) 1 SCC 177, and Article 20(1).

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_benami_transact: A person is prosecuted for a transaction alleged to be benami.
predicates.transaction_predates_amended_law: The alleged transaction occurred before the amended criminal rules came into force.
predicates.earlier_criminal_rule_is_unconstitutiona: The earlier criminal provision that might otherwise have applied to the transaction has been declared unconstitutional.

issues.definition: When a benami prosecution concerns a transaction predating the amended law and the earlier offence is unconstitutional, the rule bars retrospective criminal liability.

issues.legal_issue: Confiscation under the amended law is punitive when applied to transactions predating that law and therefore cannot operate retroactively.
material_facts: The property transaction occurred before the amended law came into force, when the earlier acquisition provision was unconstitutional and unused.
The amended scheme permits in rem confiscation of the property and its proceeds through proceedings independent of a criminal prosecution.
Confiscation transfers the taint of the transaction to the property itself and may reach proceeds that include later, legitimate additions of wealth.
The Government initiated proceedings against the company and provisionally attached the property based on the earlier transaction.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that amended-law confiscation is punitive when applied retroactively to earlier transactions and can operate only prospectively; the authorities could not initiate or continue confiscation proceedings for transactions predating the amended law.
issues.legal_principle: A provision labelled civil cannot be applied retroactively to evade Article 20(1) if, in its nature and effect, it imposes punitive forfeiture. The Court considered the criteria in Engel v. The Netherlands (No. 1), [1976] 1 EHRR 647, and Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez, 372 U.S. 144 (1963), and relied on State of West Bengal v. S.K. Ghosh, AIR 1963 SC 255, Divisional Forest Officer v. G.V. Sudhakar Rao, (1985) 4 SCC 573, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kallo Bai, (2017) 14 SCC 502, and Yogendra Kumar Jaiswal v. State of Bihar, (2016) 3 SCC 183, in examining the character and operation of forfeiture proceedings. Article 20(1) applies to punitive provisions notwithstanding their civil form.

predicates.confiscation_proceeding_under_amended_sc: An authority seeks confiscation under an amended statutory scheme governing alleged benami property.
predicates.transaction_predates_amended_law: The transaction underlying the confiscation proceeding occurred before the amended law came into force.
predicates.forfeiture_is_independent_of_criminal_co: The confiscation proceeding can result in forfeiture without a prior criminal conviction for the underlying conduct.
predicates.forfeiture_taints_property_or_proceeds: The scheme treats the property or its proceeds as tainted and makes them liable to forfeiture because of the alleged transaction.

issues.definition: When independent confiscation proceedings target property or proceeds because of a transaction predating the amended law, the rule bars retroactive confiscation.

issues.legal_issue: Show-cause, prosecution and confiscation proceedings concerning transactions predating the amended law cannot be maintained.
material_facts: The company acquired the property before the amended law came into force.
The authorities later issued a show-cause notice alleging that the property was benami and provisionally attached it under the amended scheme.

The proceedings rested on the earlier transaction, and the Court held that the earlier criminal and acquisition provisions were unconstitutional and that retroactive criminal liability and confiscation were impermissible.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the authorities could not initiate or continue criminal prosecution or confiscation proceedings for transactions predating the amended law and directed that all such proceedings stand quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 20(1) bars retroactive criminal liability and punitive confiscation; the unconstitutional earlier provisions cannot support proceedings, and the amended substantive scheme operates prospectively. The Court applied Article 20(1), T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe, (1983) 1 SCC 177, and its conclusions on the unconstitutionality of the earlier criminal and acquisition provisions.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_benami_enforcement: A proceeding challenges government action to enforce benami-transaction restrictions against identified property or persons.
predicates.underlying_transaction_predates_amended_: The transaction relied on by the authorities occurred before the amended law came into force.
predicates.action_seeks_prosecution_or_confiscation: The challenged enforcement action seeks criminal prosecution or confiscation of property.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns enforcement action seeking prosecution or confiscation based on a transaction predating the amended law, the rule requires the proceeding to be quashed.
